newsitem.title: NORWAY: BRAATHENS SAFE DOUBLES H1 OPERATING PROFIT.
newsitem.headline: BRAATHENS SAFE DOUBLES H1 OPERATING PROFIT.

text.p: Norwegian airline Braathens SAFE ASA, a competitor to Scandinavian Airlines System (SAS), on Thursday posted operating profits for the first half at 230 million crowns, almost double the year-ago result of 118 million crowns.
The company attributed the improvement to a 14 percent gain in revenues to 2.36 billion crowns and a one-off profit of 85 million crowns from the sale of three aircraft.
Braathens shares on the Oslo bourse rose strongly in early trade, advancing almost 17 percent by 1000 GMT to stand 12 crowns up at 84 crowns.

Operating expenses for the period increased 11 percent to two billion crowns against 1.80 billion crowns, mainly due to a rise in the number of employees, wage increases, higher fuel costs and an increase in expenses for handling services and other specisl services.

"Although the gross operating margin thus has improved from 13.4 percent for last year's first six-month period to 15 percent, it still fails to meet our objective of 18 percent," Braathens said in a statement.

The figures do not include earnings from Braathens' 50 percent shareholding in Swedish carrier Transwede Airways AB, which was included in the company's accounts from September 1, 1996. Due to the lack of comparitive figures for Transwede before September, Braathens produces two sets of accounts.
The company said passenger traffic between January and June grew 3.4 percent compared with a four percent rise in the total number of passengers on domestic Norwegian routes.
"..Our share of the domestic market has thus decreased marginally," it said.

However, the group's income from domestic routes increased by 13 percent, reflecting an increase in yield, in terms of income per passenger per kilometer travelled, from 1.58 crowns to 1.75 crowns, it said.
Quarter-on-quarter comparisons were skewed by the sale in the second quarter 1996 of 200,000 round-trip tickets on domestic flights linked to Braathens' 50-year jubilee.

The special-price tickets, although a boost to passenger numbers, cut revenues and reduced the domestic yield in the period to as low as 1.47 crowns. The domestic yield in the second-quarter 1997 was 1.73 crowns, while passenger traffic in July this year fell 4.9 percent from a year ago.
Braathens said it expected strong growth in the passenger income on international routes, which totalled 205 million crowns in the 1997 period versus 149 million crowns.
For the year the company said it expected a higher yield to improve the gross operating margin compared with 1996.
